How EPF Is Calculated

Your contribution = 12% of PF wages
Employer's EPF share = 12% of PF wages − EPS
EPS = 8.33% of wages, on up to ₹15,000 a month

Interest accrues on your balance each month and is credited at the end of the year. Each month's contribution starts earning from the following month.

Example: Age 30, with ₹50,000 a month in basic pay, 6% yearly raises and PF on full basic until 58. You contribute ₹49,34,024, your employer adds ₹45,14,192 to EPF, and interest adds ₹1,61,86,156, for a balance of about ₹2,56,34,372.

That balance is in future rupees. Inflation over 28 years will reduce what it can buy.

How to Use This Calculator

  1. Enter your age and retirement age
  2. Enter your basic pay plus DA and your expected yearly raise
  3. Choose how PF is calculated. A ₹1,800 monthly deduction on your payslip usually means the wage ceiling applies
  4. Add your current balance from your EPF passbook

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the current EPF interest rate?
The rate for FY 2025-26 is 8.25%, as ratified by the government in June 2026. The rate is reviewed every year, so a long-term projection is only an estimate.
How much do my employer and I contribute to EPF?
Generally you each contribute 12% of basic pay plus DA. Of the employer's share, 8.33% of wages goes to the Employees' Pension Scheme, up to ₹1,250 a month on the ₹15,000 wage ceiling, and the rest goes to your EPF.
What is the EPF wage ceiling?
It is ₹15,000 a month. Contributions are mandatory up to that level for covered employees, though many employers contribute on full basic pay. An increase has been discussed, but we found no notification of a change as of November 2026.
Is EPF interest taxable?
Interest on your own contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year is generally taxable, or above ₹5 lakh where your employer does not contribute. This calculator does not deduct that tax, so high earners may end up with somewhat less.
Is the EPF withdrawal tax-free?
Generally yes, after five continuous years of service. Earlier withdrawals can be taxed, with some exceptions such as a job loss due to ill health. Check the current rules before you withdraw.
